analysis.one_liner: Permanently protects millions of acres of Utah's red rock canyon country as wilderness.
analysis.headline: The bill had 117 cosponsors, including 14 Republicans, and held hearings in Utah — but never came to a vote before the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would designate roughly 5.6 million acres of federal land in Utah — desert mountains, canyon country, and archaeologically rich mesa lands managed by the Bureau of Land Management — as wilderness, the strictest form of public-land protection. Once designated, the land stays wild forever: no roads, no logging, no new mining or oil and gas leases, and no motorized vehicles. The bill also reserves federal water rights for each wilderness area so streams and springs there cannot be drained by other users. It never reached a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who uses or values federal public land: hikers, hunters, rafters, and future visitors get permanent protection for some of the country's most scenic desert — plus habitat for bighorn sheep, elk, and desert tortoise, and protection of ancient cliff dwellings and rock art from vandalism and theft. The federal government gains water rights to keep those wild areas functioning.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone who uses Utah's public lands

how_it_helps.text: Designates wilderness in ten Utah regions — the Great Basin, Zion-Mojave, Grand Staircase-Kaiparowits, Escalante Canyons, Henry Mountains, Dirty Devil River, Cedar Mesa, Canyonlands, San Rafael Swell, and Book Cliffs-Uinta Basin — as part of the National Wilderness Preservation System.

Wilderness status bars new roads, mineral development, and motorized vehicles on the land, keeping it open for quiet recreation like hiking, hunting, and floating rivers, per the bill's own findings on big game hunting, float trips, and canoeing.

The bill reserves enough federal water for each wilderness area, with the Interior Department required to defend those rights in Utah courts, so the wild rivers and springs the land depends on cannot be depleted by other users.
The findings note Cedar Mesa's cliff dwellings and rock art 'cry out for protection from the vandalism and theft' — designation protects the nation's archaeological heritage.

analysis.who_pays: Companies and individuals with claims on that land: mining and oil and gas interests lose access to potential deposits, and off-road vehicle users lose motorized routes. Grazing under valid existing rights is left untouched, since the bill is expressly subject to valid existing rights.
analysis.who_pays_short: Mining and oil interests; off-road vehicle users

drawbacks.text: Wilderness designation is permanent and strict: it forecloses future mining, drilling, and road building on about 5.6 million acres with no flexibility if mineral prices or needs change, and it ends motorized access on those lands, which off-road recreation users view as a loss of public-land access they currently enjoy.

Supporters of development argue that locking up large blocks of federal land removes jobs and revenue that rural Utah counties could otherwise draw from extractive industries — the bill never held a recorded vote, so Congress never weighed this trade-off on the merits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is durable and broad: permanent public ownership of spectacular federal land for quiet recreation, wildlife, and archaeology, paid for mostly by deferred development on land the public already owns. The real cost is borne narrowly by extractive industries and motorized users, and the designation's permanence means the trade-offs cannot easily be revisited. On balance the bill protected a public asset at the expense of private development interests, though a fair up-or-down debate never happened.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Resources Committee and its National Parks subcommittee, got hearings in Utah and in Washington, and then was cross-referenced to a rival Utah lands bill — it never reached a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Maurice Hinchey introduced the America's Red Rock Wilderness Act of 1995 on April 7, 1995, and it was referred to the House Committee on Resources.
It gathered 117 cosponsors — 102 Democrats, 14 Republicans, and 1 Independent — within its first months.

The committee referred it to the Subcommittee on National Parks, Forests and Lands, requested comment from the Interior Department, and held field hearings in Cedar City and Salt Lake City, Utah, plus subcommittee hearings in June 1995.

Its final action, on July 18, 1995, was a cross-reference to H.R. 1745, a competing Utah public lands bill backed by the Utah delegation; H.R. 1500 itself was never reported out of committee or brought to the floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies and users who wanted to keep developing or driving on Utah's BLM land were better off: the wilderness designation never happened, and the land remained open to mining claims, drilling proposals, and off-road use under existing law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Those wanting development access to Utah's public lands

for.name: Rep. Maurice Hinchey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a large bipartisan cosponsor list.

against.name: Rep. Don Young
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee vote or brought it to the House floor.

against.name: Rep. James Hansen
against.role: Chair, Subcommittee on National Parks, Forests and Lands
against.what_they_did: Chaired the subcommittee that held the bill's hearings; the committee's last action on H.R. 1500 was a cross-reference to H.R. 1745, a competing Utah lands bill.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan — 102 Democrats, 14 Republicans, and 1 Independent out of 117 — but the committee that controlled the bill's fate was run by the Republican majority, and no vote was ever scheduled.

industries.industry: Mining and oil and gas companies
industries.note: Wilderness designation permanently closes the affected federal lands to new mineral claims, leases, and development. Their loss is the public's gain under this bill, since the land stays wild and open to everyone.

Wilderness bars motorized vehicles, ending ORV and motorized route access on the designated lands. Quiet recreation users gain what ORV users lose, so the two public interests pull against each other here.

The bill protects land for hiking, hunting, rafting, and sightseeing permanently, and protects archaeological sites that draw visitors. The benefits flow to the general public rather than a single industry.
The bill is subject to valid existing rights, so existing grazing permits would generally continue inside wilderness areas, though new range improvements and motorized access would face limits.
